summary: Redwood SE walked OptiRetail through tradeoffs between Dedicated and Hosted inference focusing on noisy neighbor isolation, throughput guarantees, KV cache and batching behavior, and quantization impact on latency/quality. Customer is leaning toward a Dedicated pilot for predictable throughput but wants security/VPC details and a 2-hour benchmark with their prompt set.

Quantization (fp16/int8) impact on perf and quality
meeting_header: Date: 2026-12-02 | Time: 14:00-14:55 UTC | Duration: 55m | Platform: Zoom | Recording: yes
transcript:
[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to dig into the dedicated vs hosted question and go deeper on runtime behavior — latency, throughput, KV cache, batching and quantization. uh Liam will lead the performance pieces.
[00:12] Sarah Patel: Thanks Maya. We're primarily concerned about noisy neighbor effects and whether Dedicated gives us predictable p99 latency. We have a high-volume storefront use case, so tail latency matters.
[00:25] Liam O'Connor: yeah totally. quick agenda: 1) isolation/noisy neighbor 2) throughput guarantees and how we measure them 3) KV cache and prefix caching effects on repeat calls 4) batching strategies and 5) quantization tradeoffs. we'll leave 10 minutes for security / VPC questions.
[00:40] Daniel Ruiz: quick note — our baseline is 150 RPS with 512 token avg context and 50 token generation; p95 should be under 200ms ideally.
[00:50] Liam O'Connor: got it. so on noisy neighbor: hosted is multi-tenant, we do runtime scheduling and soft isolation, but you can see noisy neighbor effects when bursty workloads saturate the GPU scheduler or memory. Dedicated gives you physical isolation so those noisy neighbor cases are eliminated — that translates to far more stable tail latencies.
[01:15] Kevin Wang: can you quantify "far more stable"? e.g., what's the expected p99 delta?
[01:20] Liam O'Connor: good question. as an example, in our benchmarks on a 4xA100 pod serving a 7B family model, hosted multi-tenant p99 under bursty traffic can spike by ~40-80ms compared to steady-state, whereas dedicated shows p99 variance more like 5-15ms assuming same batching config and KV hit rate. that's a rough ballpark — it depends on model size, seq length, and whether other flows are saturating the I/O or NVMe.
[01:48] Sarah Patel: okay that matches our intuition. what about throughput guarantees? we need predictable tokens/sec for our SLAs.
[01:55] Liam O'Connor: Dedicated comes with reserved GPU capacity and configured throughput targets. we publish performance profiles per model — e.g., X tokens/sec for Y batch size. For hosted, we have soft SLOs and dynamic scaling but not the same hard commit on throughput. you can request burst reservations in hosted but it's not identical to Dedicated.
[02:12] Maya Chen: to add, Dedicated contracts can include throughput/latency SLAs and you'd pay for reserved capacity, and we build in automatic fallback policies so if your Dedicated pool is down we can failover to hosted variants, though that's a policy you decide on.
[02:28] Daniel Ruiz: fallback is fine but we need to understand cold starts and kv cache warmup. if we failover to hosted, do we lose the KV cache and see a big latency hit?
[02:35] Liam O'Connor: yes, good point. KV cache is local to the serving instance/pool. if you fail over to a different model variant or region, you'll be cold. typical behavior: first few requests after failover pay the cache warmup cost — those can be 2-3x higher per-token cost and latency until the KV warms. We recommend warmup plans during cutovers — e.g., route low-traffic canary that primes KV prefixes.
[03:05] Priya Mehta: can you explain how KV cache hit rates are calculated? we have lots of short conversational prefixes and hope to get high hit rates.
[03:12] Liam O'Connor: KV hit rate = number of tokens served from cached KV frames / total tokens. For repetitive prompts or shared system prefixes you often hit 60-80%. for highly unique user-driven prompts it's lower. important: batching and request shaping affect hit rate because when requests are grouped, the KV entries that are beneficial might differ. Also our runtime supports prefix dedupe and shared prefix caches per tenant in Dedicated which helps.
[03:44] Daniel Ruiz: is that prefix dedupe something only in Dedicated?
[03:47] Liam O'Connor: it's available in both, but Dedicated gives you stronger guarantees around eviction policies and cache sizes because you control the pool. In hosted we have quotas and more aggressive eviction to keep multi-tenant fairness.
[03:59] Sarah Patel: let's talk batching — we want low p95 but high throughput. how do you balance batch size and latency?
[04:05] Liam O'Connor: classic tradeoff: larger batch sizes improve GPU utilization and tokens/sec, but increase per-request latency due to queueing. we tune batching with two knobs: target batch size and max wait time. For interactive workloads you set small max wait (e.g., 10ms) and lower batch sizes. For async high-throughput, you allow 50-100ms waits and larger batches. Another lever is dynamic batching: the runtime adapts batch size to recent arrival rates to hit latency SLOs while maximizing throughput.
[04:37] Kevin Wang: Do you allow colocated batching for customer-level isolation? i.e., keep only OptiRetail requests in the batch?
[04:44] Liam O'Connor: yes, in Dedicated we can do tenant-only batching which eliminates cross-tenant noise and prioritization issues. In hosted, batches are mixed for efficiency unless you purchase dedicated lanes.
[04:55] Sarah Patel: quantization — we have quality targets on some prompts. what's the latency/accuracy tradeoff between fp16 and int8 quant?
[05:02] Liam O'Connor: fp16 is the baseline on GPUs, gives you fast perf with minimal quality change for most models. int8 (or qat/LLM-int8) can yield 1.6x-2.5x speedups and memory reductions but may introduce subtle quality regressions, especially on long-context tasks or models with sensitive numeric reasoning. We recommend running evals/prompt sets to measure ROUGE/BLEU or custom metrics. In Dedicated you can run multiple quantized variants and A/B them with rollout policies.
[05:33] Daniel Ruiz: for our recommendation layer, slight hallucination uptick is a no-go on 1% of cases. We'll need evaluation.
[05:38] Liam O'Connor: understood — we can run quantization experiments in the pilot: int8 on a replica and compare logits/outputs to fp16 for your prompt set and flag regressions.
[05:48] Maya Chen: also note we have quantization profiles per model architecture — not all int8 paths are equal. for some community models we've validated linear quant → stable outputs, for others there's more noise.
[05:58] Sarah Patel: how about on-prem / VPC connectors — we need to know which network ports, if peering is possible, and data residency constraints.
[06:06] Maya Chen: for Private / on-prem we ship a control-plane lightweight agent that communicates over TLS outbound, and compute sits in your VPC. For VPC peering we support AWS VPC peering and PrivateLink; we also support customer-managed KMS/HSM for key control. We'll share a network checklist.
[06:24] Kevin Wang: any extra latency introduced by the control plane?
[06:28] Liam O'Connor: minimal — inference data paths are local. control-plane calls are for management, metrics, and model pulls. Runtime path is direct GPU path. If you proxy through additional NAT gateways you may add a few ms but it's negligible compared to model inference times.
[06:42] Daniel Ruiz: for Dedicated, what's the failure mode? if a GPU in the pool dies, do requests fail, or do you reroute?
[06:49] Liam O'Connor: we monitor node health and will drain failing nodes and route to the remaining pool. in practice we maintain headroom in Dedicated pools to absorb single-node failures. fallback options: 1) route to other Dedicated nodes in same pool 2) route to a warm standby in another zone or hosted. the key is having a warm standby with warmed KV or priming plan.
[07:12] Sarah Patel: can we get a performance profile doc per model? we need numbers (tokens/sec, typical p50/p95/p99) for the model sizes we care about.
[07:20] Maya Chen: yes, we'll attach model performance sheets. Liam — I think you already have a perf matrix we can share.
[07:25] Liam O'Connor: will do, I'll include batch sizes and sequence length samples.
[07:30] Priya Mehta: on instrumentation — how do we get per-route breakdowns and token-level cost traces?
[07:36] Maya Chen: Redwood Console provides per-route latency and cost breakdowns, plus traces per-request. You can export to Datadog or BigQuery. For Dedicated we give higher-resolution metrics and longer retention as an add-on.
[07:48] Daniel Ruiz: latency SLOs — can the Dedicated contract include p95 < 150ms for our config?
[07:55] Maya Chen: yes as long as the requested capacity aligns with the throughput; we'll size the pool for your 150 RPS with target p95 and include that in the scope. SLA language is negotiable.
[08:05] Kevin Wang: what about eviction and cache sizing? we have keys with long lifetimes and some with heavy churn.
[08:12] Liam O'Connor: in Dedicated you set cache size and TTLs; we expose eviction metrics. For heavy churn workloads, we recommend small per-user TTLs and prefetching for hot prefixes. Also consider local SSD-backed KV for very large caches. In hosted we limit cache sizes per-tenant to prevent runaway memory.
[08:34] Sarah Patel: any gotchas with long context windows and KV? we plan to move to 8k contexts later this quarter.
[08:41] Liam O'Connor: longer contexts increase KV size and KV lookup times slightly, but the runtime optimizes retrieval. quantization interacts with memory (int8 reduces memory, good for long contexts). also kernel selection changes — some attention kernels are better at longer seqs. We'll make kernel recommendations per model/seq length.
[09:02] Priya Mehta: do you support hybrid setups — e.g., Dedicated for peak daytime traffic, hosted for night or overflow?
[09:09] Liam O'Connor: yes, that's a common pattern. smart routing can send primary traffic to Dedicated and overflow to hosted; add warm-up policies to mitigate cold caches. Also you can use traffic shaping and priority lanes.
[09:22] Daniel Ruiz: in that overflow case, how do you ensure consistency in model versions and tokenization?
[09:28] Liam O'Connor: we ensure model artifacts are identical across pools; tokenizers are packaged with the model. version pinning is configurable. The main inconsistency is cache state, not the model outputs (unless you run different quantized variants). For consistency you can pin both to fp16 or pin to quantized variant across pools.
[09:46] Sarah Patel: what's typical turnaround to get a Dedicated pilot?
[09:50] Maya Chen: depends on region and capacity; usually 2-4 weeks for onboarding and capacity allocation assuming no special compliance constraints. If you need on-prem, that can take longer due to network and security approvals.
[09:59] Kevin Wang: ok. for the pilot you'll run benchmarks — can you outline what you'll measure?
[10:03] Liam O'Connor: yes: steady-state tokens/sec at target batch size, p50/p95/p99 latencies under your traffic shape, cold-warm cache comparisons, KV hit rate, and quality delta for quantized variants. We'll produce CSVs and a summary sheet.
[10:16] Daniel Ruiz: we'll supply traffic shape and prompt set. Do you need deterministic seeds for generation?
[10:20] Liam O'Connor: if you want deterministic comparisons, yes we'll fix seeds and decoding params across runs. For business metrics we often do temperature 0 and greedy/top-k comparatives.
[10:30] Sarah Patel: any security items we should flag now? SSO, audit logs, data retention.
[10:35] Maya Chen: for Private and Dedicated we support SAML SSO, role-based access, audit logs export, and KMS integration. We'll include the security pack and compliance artifacts.
[10:46] Priya Mehta: pricing — dedicated pricing model details we'll discuss with finance but want a ballpark.
[10:51] Maya Chen: we'll send a pricing sheet after this call. pilot pricing is usually discounted.
[10:55] Liam O'Connor: ok last technical note — quantization A/B should include quality gates: if top-k token overlap falls below threshold or a custom metric regresses >X% we hold rollout. We can automate that.
[11:08] Daniel Ruiz: good. Also interested in tooling for flushing or preloading KV for deployments.
[11:12] Liam O'Connor: we expose APIs to prime KV, evict keys, and import/export cache snapshots in Dedicated. Those are admin-only ops.
[11:20] Sarah Patel: ok let's recap and next steps.
[11:23] Maya Chen: recap: Redwood will run a 2-hour Dedicated benchmark (Liam) with OptiRetail's prompts once provided; Maya to send SOC2 and VPC/network checklist; Daniel to upload prompts and traffic shape; we'll schedule pilot kickoff.
[11:36] Kevin Wang: thanks everyone, will follow up on the firewall items.
[11:40] Maya Chen: thanks all, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the datasheets.
[11:45] [Recording ends]
